sources.quote: "Stress in the Poqomchi' language is fixed and falls on the last syllable, except in some words coming from Spanish which keep their own stress. Because of the fixed position of stress it is not written orthographically."

sources.citation: Weichel, Lindsay Anne (2006). The grammatical structure of Western Pokomchi'. M.A. thesis, University of Regina. xiii+187 pp. hdl:10294/13397 (open, uregina.scholaris.ca)
sources.quote: 'The most prominent phonetic correlate of stress is pitch, as stressed syllables are articulated with a higher pitch than unstressed syllables... Word stress is generally predictable in Pokomchi', as it falls almost exclusively on the last syllable in a word, regardless of the syllable weight of this syllable' (exx. 2.58-2.63 [kamaníkh] 'to work', [tinamít] 'town'); 'There are few exceptions to this, most of which are borrowings from Spanish' ([méša] 'table', [wákaš] 'cow'); one native exception /čáxari/ 'What?' explained as a fossilized phrase. sources.quote: 'Stress is predictable in Mayan languages, with few exceptions... Fixed final stress: K'ichean-branch Mayan languages and Southern Mam.' Family-level; no Poqomchi'-specific data.

sources.quote: 'Final stress (36a) is the norm in K'ichean languages' (Poqomchi' is K'ichean; no Poqomchi'-specific stress statement). Also notes fieldworkers' impression that stress is stronger phrase/utterance-finally in final-stress languages but that 'stress is phonologically present at the word level even when acoustically weak' — relevant to the StressTyp2/Mayers word-vs-phrase lumping.
